entries.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
entries.lesson_core_move: Derive the Fourier-domain output relation $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ by applying the Fourier transform to the LTI convolution equation and identifying $H(j\omega)$ as the transform of the impulse response.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.learning_goal: Orient the learner to the convolution description of an LTI output and preview why the Fourier transform turns that description into a product.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that the lesson starts from the standard LTI convolution equation and that the frequency-domain result will come from transforming that equation, not from introducing a new system model.
tutorial_outline.base_case: One continuous-time LTI system with input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$, with the output written in its standard convolution form.
paragraph_plan: State the LTI setting and remind the reader that the output is determined by the impulse response.
Write the convolution equation $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ and its integral form as the starting point for the lesson.
Explain that the next steps will transform both sides and use the convolution theorem to move from time-domain convolution to frequency-domain multiplication.
Preview the final relation $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ and note that $H(j\omega)$ names the transform of $h(t)$.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction brief, algebraic, and forward-looking. Do not add practice here; the goal is to set up the convolution equation that the example sections will transform.

sections.section_title: Writing the LTI Output as a Convolution
sections.learning_goal: Rewrite the output of an LTI system as a convolution integral using standard notation.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct convolution expression.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which expression correctly writes the output $y(t)$ of an LTI system with input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$ as a convolution?
distractor_plan: Include the compact but incorrect product $y(t)=x(t)h(t)$.
Include the factors in the wrong order or with the wrong shift sign.
Include an expression that omits the integral or its bounds.
Include a choice that uses frequency-domain notation too early.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given an LTI system with input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$, write the output $y(t)$ as a convolution integral.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Convert the system description into $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the introductory framing to the first concrete symbolic rewrite.
solution_step_plan: State the LTI output relation in convolution form.
Expand the convolution into its integral notation.
Keep the input, impulse response, and output variables distinct.
Confirm that this is the time-domain starting point for the frequency-domain derivation.
practice_variation_axes: Change the names of the input and impulse response while keeping the same convolution structure.
Ask for the equivalent integral form instead of the compact convolution symbol.
Include a near-miss option with the wrong shift sign or with the factors swapped.
Vary whether the question asks for the output equation or the convolution operator notation.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as the first concrete rewrite. Later questions should stay symbolic and test recognition of the correct convolution form and obvious near-miss errors.

sections.section_title: Applying the Fourier Transform to the Convolution Equation
sections.learning_goal: Apply the Fourier transform to the convolution equation without changing the system model.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct transformed relation.
question_policy.practice_question_model: After taking the Fourier transform of the convolution equation, which relation appears before simplification?
distractor_plan: Use the original time-domain convolution as an answer choice.
Use a direct product $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ too early.
Use a transform applied to only one factor in the convolution.
Confuse $Y(j\omega)$ with $y(t)$ or reverse the frequency variable.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Starting from $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, apply the Fourier transform to both sides and write the transformed relation.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Set up the transformed equation $Y(j\omega)$ on the left and keep the right-hand side in a form ready for the convolution theorem.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds one transform step to the convolution equation without yet simplifying it.
solution_step_plan: Apply the Fourier transform to $y(t)$ and name the left-hand side $Y(j\omega)$.
Write the transformed right-hand side as the Fourier transform of the convolution integral.
Keep the notation symbolic so the theorem can be invoked in the next step.
Stop before substituting any specific transform pair.
practice_variation_axes: Ask for the transformed equation immediately after applying $\mathcal{F}$.
Vary whether the equation is presented in compact or integral form.
Include a distractor that treats the transform of a convolution as a product before the theorem is named.
Swap the roles of input and output symbols to test notation tracking.

sections.handoff_notes: The example should stop before the convolution theorem is used. Later questions should probe the transformed relation, not the final product.

sections.section_title: Using the Convolution Theorem on the Output Spectrum
sections.learning_goal: Replace the transformed convolution structure with the frequency-domain product of the two transforms.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct frequency-domain product.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which frequency-domain expression replaces the transformed convolution after applying the convolution theorem?
distractor_plan: Include the unsimplified transformed convolution as a choice.
Include a frequency-domain convolution instead of multiplication.
Include a sum of spectra rather than a product.
Include a choice that drops the transform notation or changes the variable names.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Take the transformed convolution relation from the previous step and simplify it using the convolution theorem.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Replace the transformed convolution structure with the frequency-domain product of the two spectra.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from raw transform notation to the theorem-based simplification.
solution_step_plan: Recognize the transformed convolution as the pattern covered by the convolution theorem.
Replace the transformed convolution with a product of spectra.
Keep the same frequency variable throughout the simplification.
State the simplified output relation in frequency form.
practice_variation_axes: Vary whether the question gives the theorem statement or the transformed equation.
Use a product-versus-convolution distractor.
Vary the notation for the frequency variable while keeping the algebra the same.
Ask for the simplified expression rather than the theorem name.

sections.handoff_notes: This should be the minimal theorem application. Later questions should distinguish convolution from multiplication in frequency.

sections.section_title: Identifying $H(j\omega)$ as the Transform of $h(t)$
sections.learning_goal: Name the transform of the impulse response and connect it to the system frequency response notation.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct transform identity.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What notation names the Fourier transform of the impulse response $h(t)$?
distractor_plan: Use $X(j\omega)$ or $Y(j\omega)$ in place of $H(j\omega)$.
Use $h(j\omega)$ or $H(t)$ instead of the correct transform notation.
Treat the impulse response itself as the spectrum.
Mix the input and system symbols in the product.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given the impulse response $h(t)$, identify its Fourier transform $H(j\omega)$ and substitute it into the output relation.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Name the transform of the impulse response and connect it to the system frequency response notation.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds the naming step that turns the generic frequency-domain product into a system-specific expression.
solution_step_plan: Define $H(j\omega)=\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$.
Substitute $H(j\omega)$ into the product form from the previous step.
Interpret $H(j\omega)$ as the frequency response of the LTI system.
Keep the notation aligned with the input spectrum $X(j\omega)$ and output spectrum $Y(j\omega)$.
practice_variation_axes: Ask for the correct transform notation of the impulse response.
Vary between naming the transform and substituting it into a relation.
Include distractors that confuse $h(t)$ with $H(j\omega)$ or with $X(j\omega)$.
Ask for the expression that makes the system-response meaning explicit.

sections.handoff_notes: The key move is naming and substituting $H(j\omega)$ correctly. Later questions should test symbol identity, not calculus.

sections.section_title: Deriving $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$
sections.learning_goal: Combine the prior steps into the completed frequency-domain output formula for an LTI system.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic answer choices with one correct final relation.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Which equation correctly completes the derivation of the Fourier-domain output relation for an LTI system?
distractor_plan: Include the time-domain convolution instead of the final frequency-domain relation.
Include an incorrect operation such as addition or division between $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$.
Include a relation with the wrong left-hand-side symbol, such as $x(t)$ or $y(t)$.
Include a product that omits the impulse-response transform notation.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Starting from the convolution equation and the definition of $H(j\omega)$, derive the final relation $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Combine the time-domain convolution, the Fourier transform, and the convolution theorem into the completed output formula.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Synthesizes all previous steps into the lesson's final identity.
solution_step_plan: Write the output as a convolution integral.
Apply the Fourier transform to both sides.
Use the convolution theorem to replace the transformed convolution with a product.
Substitute $H(j\omega)=\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$ and conclude with $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
practice_variation_axes: Ask for the completed final identity after a partial derivation.
Vary the form of the prompt: direct equation, fill-in-the-blank, or choose the correct completion.
Include close distractors that use addition, division, or the wrong transform symbol.
Ask for the relation in the same notation but with a different ordering of the derivation steps.

sections.handoff_notes: This should read as the lesson's synthesis step. Later questions should focus on completing or selecting the derived identity.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the time-domain output of an LTI system by forming $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, simplifying the product, and applying the inverse Fourier transform.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Finding Output with $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$
sections.learning_goal: Introduce the minimum frequency-domain procedure for an LTI output: identify $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$, form $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, and invert to $y(t)$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the lesson is purely symbolic and uses Fourier-transform notation only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. Keep the tutorial focused on the convolution theorem, the product $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, and the inverse Fourier transform.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions for the tutorial section; this is direct instruction only.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Not applicable.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the procedure in the smallest usable form: start from the LTI input-output relation, identify $H(j\omega)$ as the transform of $h(t)$, multiply $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$, then apply the inverse Fourier transform to recover $y(t)$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A simple LTI system with a known input spectrum and a simple system response, where the only new move is to turn the frequency-domain product back into a time-domain output.
paragraph_plan: Open by stating that an LTI system turns convolution in time into multiplication in frequency, so the output spectrum is found by forming $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
Show that $H(j\omega)$ comes from the impulse response $h(t)$, so the system is represented by a standard transform pair rather than by a new time-domain operation.
Lay out the operational sequence the learner should repeat: multiply the spectra, simplify only as needed, and then invert the result to get $y(t)$.
Keep the first pass small and concrete so the learner can attach the theorem to one clean algebraic procedure instead of a full derivation.
Close by transitioning immediately to worked practice so the learner applies the procedure before the explanation gets abstract.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial concise and procedural. The writer should establish the theorem, the product rule, and the inverse-transform step, then hand off quickly to active practice.

sections.section_title: Forming $Y(j\omega)$ from $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$
sections.learning_goal: Multiply the input spectrum and system response correctly to form $Y(j\omega)$ without simplifying away the structure yet.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is a symbolic multiplication of spectra.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. The worked example and follow-up questions should stay in symbolic form only.

question_policy.answer_format: Select the one symbolic product that equals $Y(j\omega)$.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{j\omega+1}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{2}{j\omega+3}$, which expression is the correct unsimplified form of $Y(j\omega)$?
distractor_plan: Include one choice that multiplies only the numerators or only the denominators and drops a factor.
Include one choice that adds $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ instead of multiplying them.
Include one choice that swaps the factor order but keeps an algebraic mistake such as a missing constant.
Include one choice that jumps ahead and simplifies or cancels a factor that is not actually cancelable.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{j\omega+1}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{2}{j\omega+3}$, form $Y(j\omega)$ in product form.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Write $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ exactly and preserve the factors so the next step can simplify them.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Compared with the tutorial, this removes the verbal explanation and asks the learner to execute the first algebraic move on concrete spectra.
solution_step_plan: Identify the given $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$.
Substitute both expressions into $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
Leave the result in clean product form rather than simplifying it.
practice_variation_axes: Change the pole locations in $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$.
Swap which factor carries the gain constant.
Vary whether the product has one or two denominator factors while keeping the multiplication structure the same.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the first example at the product stage only. Do not introduce cancellation or inverse transforms yet.

sections.section_title: Simplifying the Frequency-Domain Product
sections.learning_goal: Simplify a formed product for $Y(j\omega)$ by canceling shared factors and rewriting it in a transform-ready form.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is algebraic simplification of a rational spectrum.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. Keep the focus on cancellation and algebraic cleanup before inversion.

question_policy.answer_format: Select the fully simplified symbolic form of $Y(j\omega)$.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $Y(j\omega)=\frac{2(j\omega+4)}{(j\omega+1)(j\omega+2)}\cdot\frac{j\omega+1}{j\omega+4}$, which expression is the simplified result?
distractor_plan: Include one choice that leaves the cancelable factor unreduced.
Include one choice that cancels the wrong factor or cancels a factor that is only present once.
Include one choice that moves the gain constant to the denominator or inverts the remaining fraction.
Include one choice with a sign error in the surviving pole term.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $Y(j\omega)=\frac{2(j\omega+4)}{(j\omega+1)(j\omega+2)}\cdot\frac{j\omega+1}{j\omega+4}$, simplify the product before inversion.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Cancel the shared factor, reduce the rational expression, and leave $Y(j\omega)$ in a form ready for inverse-transform matching.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Compared with section 2, the product now contains a cancelable factor, so the learner has to reduce the algebra before inversion.
solution_step_plan: Write the product in a single rational form and identify the shared factor.
Cancel the common factor cleanly and keep the remaining constant visible.
Rewrite the reduced expression so it is immediately usable in the next inverse-transform step.
practice_variation_axes: Introduce one cancelable factor.
Move the remaining scale factor outside the fraction.
Change the surviving pole so the learner has to recognize the simplified form rather than memorize a template.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the algebraic cleanup stage. The writer should emphasize cancellation and a transform-ready result, not inversion yet.

sections.section_title: Inverting $Y(j\omega)$ Using a Known Transform Pair
sections.learning_goal: Recognize a standard Fourier transform pair in $Y(j\omega)$ and invert it directly to obtain $y(t)$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is to match a single spectrum to a known inverse-transform pair.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. The example should stay focused on pair recognition and the inverse transform.

question_policy.answer_format: Select the time-domain signal whose Fourier transform is the given $Y(j\omega)$.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $Y(j\omega)=\frac{2}{j\omega+2}$, which time-domain signal is $y(t)$?
distractor_plan: Include one choice with the wrong exponential rate, such as $e^{-t}u(t)$ instead of $e^{-2t}u(t)$.
Include one choice that omits the unit step $u(t)$.
Include one choice that uses a sinusoidal or even-signal pair instead of the causal exponential pair.
Include one choice that keeps the correct shape but puts the constant in the wrong place.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $Y(j\omega)=\frac{2}{j\omega+2}$, use the standard pair for $e^{-at}u(t)$ to find $y(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Match the simplified spectrum to a standard pair and write the corresponding inverse transform with the correct causal factor.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Compared with section 3, the learner now stops after simplification and converts one clean term back to the time domain.
solution_step_plan: Identify $Y(j\omega)$ as a standard single-pole transform pair.
Match the parameter value in the denominator to the time-domain decay rate.
Apply the inverse Fourier transform and write the output signal in time domain.
practice_variation_axes: Change the decay constant in $a+j\omega$.
Vary the scalar multiple on the transform pair.
Keep the inverse pair single-term so the learner practices recognition rather than decomposition.

sections.handoff_notes: This section is a single-pair inverse-transform exercise. Keep the algebra minimal and the pair recognition explicit.

sections.section_title: Finding $y(t)$ from a Decomposed Frequency-Domain Product
sections.learning_goal: Decompose a rational $Y(j\omega)$ into standard transform pairs, invert each term, and combine the pieces by linearity.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is a symbolic partial-fraction decomposition followed by inverse transforms.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a visual. The example should show decomposition, pair matching, and linearity only.

question_policy.answer_format: Select the time-domain output after decomposing $Y(j\omega)$ into standard inverse-transform terms.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $Y(j\omega)=\frac{2}{(j\omega+1)(j\omega+3)}$, which time-domain signal is $y(t)$ after partial fractions and inverse transforming each term?
distractor_plan: Include one choice with incorrect partial-fraction coefficients.
Include one choice that inverts only one term and drops the other.
Include one choice that uses the right exponentials but the wrong sign between them.
Include one choice that omits the unit step $u(t)$ from one or both terms.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $Y(j\omega)=\frac{2}{(j\omega+1)(j\omega+3)}$, decompose it into standard terms and find $y(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Split $Y(j\omega)$ into two standard transform terms, invert each term separately, and combine the time-domain results by linearity.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Compared with section 4, the output spectrum is no longer a single table entry; the learner must decompose it and then invert term by term.
solution_step_plan: Rewrite the rational function in partial-fraction form.
Solve for the coefficients so each term matches a standard Fourier transform pair.
Invert each term separately and add the results to get $y(t)$.
practice_variation_axes: Change the two pole locations.
Change the numerator constant so the coefficients are not symmetric.
Require two-term decomposition and termwise inversion rather than a single direct pair.

sections.handoff_notes: This is the culminating synthesis step. The writer should show partial fractions, inverse-pair matching, and linearity in a compact sequence.

entries.lesson_title: Comparing Direct Convolution and Frequency-Domain Multiplication
entries.lesson_core_move: Choose between direct convolution and frequency-domain multiplication by comparing the time-domain overlap integral with the transform-pair, multiplication, and inverse-transform workload.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Comparing Direct Convolution and Frequency-Domain Multiplication
sections.learning_goal: Set up the comparison between direct convolution and frequency-domain multiplication so the learner chooses the shorter LTI workflow before computing.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image. Keep the comparison purely symbolic so the learner can count the work in each method.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach the learner to compare the workload of $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ with the workload of $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ before choosing a method for an LTI output.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a case where the convolution overlap is a single simple interval and the frequency-domain route is also available, so the method choice comes from counting steps instead of from hidden tricks.
paragraph_plan: State the two valid LTI output routes: direct convolution in time and multiplication in frequency.
Explain that the decision is about workload, not about which formula is more "correct".
Describe the direct-convolution workload: find the overlap interval, set the bounds, and evaluate the integral piecewise if needed.
Describe the frequency-domain workload: look up or derive transform pairs, multiply spectra, and check whether the inverse transform is immediate or messy.
Conclude with the rule: choose the shorter symbolic path, and let difficult bounds or a hard inverse transform tip the decision.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial to the minimum effective dose: define both routes, define the comparison rule, and hand off to the examples without solving a full output problem.

sections.section_title: Comparing Workloads When the Time-Domain Overlap Is Simple
sections.learning_goal: Choose direct convolution when the overlap integral is short and the frequency-domain route adds more bookkeeping than it removes.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image. The decision can be made entirely from symbolic supports and workload counts.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices labeled A-E; choose the single easier workflow.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$, which method is easier for finding $y(t)$: direct convolution or frequency-domain multiplication?
distractor_plan: Offer frequency-domain multiplication as the tempting opposite choice when the learner overvalues the transform formula.
Include a choice that says both methods are equally easy even though the direct overlap integral is shorter.
Include a choice that picks frequency-domain multiplication because a transform pair exists, while ignoring the extra inverse-transform step.
Include a choice that picks direct convolution for the wrong reason, such as "convolution always works," instead of because the overlap is simple.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$, decide whether direct convolution or frequency-domain multiplication is the shorter path for finding $y(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the convolution bounds are simple enough that the time-domain integral is shorter than finding both transform pairs, multiplying, and inverting the product.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first concrete comparison after the general rule: the learner sees that compact support can make direct convolution cheaper than the frequency-domain route.
solution_step_plan: Identify the finite supports and note that the convolution overlap is limited to one simple interval.
Count the direct-convolution work: set the bounds once, integrate a simple product, and avoid extra transform bookkeeping.
Count the frequency-domain work: find both transform pairs, multiply them, and still have to invert the product.
Choose direct convolution because the time-domain route has the smaller total symbolic burden.
practice_variation_axes: Change the pulse widths while keeping compact support.
Shift one signal so the overlap interval moves but remains simple.
Replace one rectangular pulse with another piecewise-constant shape.
Vary amplitudes without changing the method-choice logic.

sections.handoff_notes: Follow the worked example with one or two method-choice questions that keep the overlap simple but change the pulse widths or shifts.

sections.section_title: Comparing Workloads When Transform Pairs Are Available
sections.learning_goal: Choose frequency-domain multiplication when the transform pairs are already known and the product simplifies faster than the convolution integral.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image. The comparison is about table lookup, multiplication, and inversion, not about a visual object.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices labeled A-E; choose the single easier workflow.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, which method is easier for finding $y(t)$: direct convolution or frequency-domain multiplication?
distractor_plan: Offer direct convolution as the tempting opposite choice when the learner focuses only on the time-domain formula.
Include a choice that says both methods are equally easy even though the transform pairs are already available.
Include a choice that picks frequency-domain multiplication but ignores the inverse-transform work needed to finish the answer.
Include a choice that picks the method with the most familiar notation rather than the lower workload.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, decide whether direct convolution or frequency-domain multiplication is the shorter path for finding $y(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that once both transform pairs are available, multiplying spectra and inverting the result is shorter than setting up the time-domain integral.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Unlike the simple-overlap case, the key feature here is that both transform pairs are available immediately, so the decision is driven by lookup and product simplification.
solution_step_plan: Identify the available transform pairs and note that the frequency-domain route starts from known formulas.
Compare the time-domain integral with the algebra needed to multiply the spectra.
Check whether the inverse transform is routine once the product is simplified.
Choose frequency-domain multiplication if it requires fewer symbolic steps overall.
practice_variation_axes: Change the decay rates while keeping the same exponential family.
Add a scale factor to one signal.
Swap in another signal with a standard transform pair.
Keep the transform pairs available but alter the algebraic simplification needed after multiplication.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example centered on the fact that the transform pairs are already known; the learner should compare total workload, not just recognize the formulas.

sections.section_title: Comparing Workloads When the Inverse Transform Is Hard
sections.learning_goal: Choose direct convolution when the frequency-domain product would require an awkward inverse transform even though the transforms themselves are available.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image. The bottleneck is the inverse transform, so the comparison should stay symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices labeled A-E; choose the single easier workflow.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, which method is easier for finding $y(t)$: direct convolution or frequency-domain multiplication?
distractor_plan: Offer frequency-domain multiplication as the tempting opposite choice because the transform pairs exist, even though the inverse transform is awkward.
Include a choice that says both methods are equally easy and ignores the hard inverse transform.
Include a choice that treats direct convolution as inferior simply because it involves an integral.
Include a choice that focuses on the neat appearance of the product instead of the cost of recovering $y(t)$.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, decide whether direct convolution or frequency-domain multiplication is the shorter path for finding $y(t)$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the frequency-domain route reaches a product quickly but leaves an inverse transform that is harder than the single finite-interval convolution integral.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example adds the opposite wrinkle from the previous one: the transform pairs are usable, but the inverse transform becomes the bottleneck.
solution_step_plan: Identify the transform pairs and note that the frequency-domain route is available.
Multiply the spectra and inspect whether the product matches a simple inverse-transform pair.
Compare that inverse-transform burden with the direct-convolution integral over one finite interval.
Choose direct convolution because it finishes with less symbolic effort.
practice_variation_axes: Change the pulse width while keeping the exponential response.
Shift the pulse so the overlap interval moves.
Adjust the exponential decay rate.
Swap in another transform pair that produces a messy inverse.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the inverse-transform burden explicit. The point is not that frequency-domain multiplication fails, but that it can be slower than a direct integral.

sections.section_title: Choosing the Easier Output Method from Both Workflows
sections.learning_goal: Compare both workflows end-to-end and choose the method with the smaller total symbolic workload.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image. The synthesis step is a symbolic comparison of total workload across both methods.

question_policy.answer_format: Five answer choices labeled A-E; choose the single easier workflow.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-3)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, which method is easier for finding $y(t)$: direct convolution or frequency-domain multiplication?
distractor_plan: Offer the opposite method as a tempting choice when the learner fixates on only one part of the workload.
Include a choice that says both methods are equally easy and ignores the total count of symbolic steps.

entries.lesson_title: Periodic Inputs Through an LTI System

sections.section_title: Introduction to Periodic Inputs Through an LTI System

sections.section_title: Scaling One Fourier-Series Harmonic by $H(jk\omega_0)$

sections.section_title: Finding Output from a Direct Aperiodic Transform Pair
sections.learning_goal: Use a direct transform pair to compute the output of a causal exponential input through a causal first-order LTI system.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic answer choices for the correct output expression
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, which expression is the correct output $y(t)$?
distractor_plan: Swap the two decay rates in the exponential difference.
Drop the unit step $u(t)$ from the final answer.
Return a single exponential instead of the difference of two exponentials.
Miss the factor that comes from partial fraction decomposition.
Confuse the input signal with the output signal.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, find $y(t)$ using the Fourier transform method.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Recognize $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$, multiply them to get $Y(j\omega)=\frac{1}{(1+j\omega)(2+j\omega)}$, and invert to $y(t)=\big(e^{-t}-e^{-2t}\big)u(t)$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first fully worked numerical example after the tutorial, so the only new work is carrying the complete transform-to-inverse cycle with a concrete aperiodic input and impulse response.
solution_step_plan: Write $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ from the transform table.
Multiply to form $Y(j\omega)$.
Use partial fractions or known pair matching to rewrite $Y(j\omega)$ as a sum of standard terms.
Invert each term and combine the results into $y(t)$.
practice_variation_axes: Change one exponential rate.
Swap the input and system decay constants.
Ask for the final $y(t)$ rather than the intermediate $Y(j\omega)$.
Keep the same rational-product structure but change the coefficient.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the example table-driven and short; the follow-up question should mirror the same transform-pair workflow with only the decay constants changed.

question_policy.answer_format: five symbolic answer choices for the correct output expression

Invert the input spectrum by itself instead of the product.
Keep the wrong pole location after cancellation.
Drop the unit step $u(t)$ from the output.

Change the zero/pole cancellation pattern in $H(j\omega)$.
Ask for $Y(j\omega)$ before inversion.
